originalTitle: Can a 6% Dividend Yield Really Last? Here’s What History Says
summary: A 6% dividend yield sounds like an income investor's dream, but the same number that makes a stock look attractive can signal something far more troubling beneath the surface. Knowing the difference before you buy could save your portfolio from a painful cut.

As soon as anyone hears the words “6% yield,” it’s going to grab a lot of attention, and for the right reasons. This is a strong return for most investors who want to generate real income and growth from a portfolio over time. This number gets even more appealing when you look at the average S&P 500 yield right now, which is sitting around 1.05%, so the opportunity to generate four times more than what the S&P is doing is undoubtedly appealing.

The challenge with hearing this yield number is that you really need to make sure you are aware of what you are getting for the yield. There are red flags that investors should be aware of, and knowing them isn’t just something to think about in passing, but they might be vital pieces of information before you start putting money into an investment.

Why High Yields Appear in the First Place

For the most part, calculating a dividend yield is pretty easy to do, as you only have to take the annual dividend and divide it by the share price. It’s pretty simple to calculate, but the reality is that a company can raise its dividend payout, something just about every investor loves to see. However, if the share price falls, it pushes the yield higher automatically without the company having to do anything.

There is another scenario, which is usually the one that 6% dividends originate from, and it’s something that you have to scrutinize a little bit more. If a stock drops, especially quickly, it’s because the market has already started pricing in something wrong beneath the surface. The rising yield is likely more a symptom of a problem, and it isn’t necessarily a reason to make a stock purchase.

The moment you start digging deeper into what dividend sustainability can look like, there is a better-than-good chance you’ll wind up with the same conclusion each time. Yields that sit above the broader market tend to get cut at a higher rate as yields move closer to what would be considered “normal” levels. To be fair, this isn’t a hard rule, but it does give us something to consider, as the companies that are paying out 6% or more of their share price are often doing it at the very edge of what their cash flow levels can actually support.

What tells the real story is the payout ratio, and a company that is paying out 90% of its earnings as dividends is often the same company that doesn’t have much of a cushion. All it takes is one bad quarter, one interest rate move, or one unexpected capital expense, and a dividend cut happens, and investors are furious. A company that is only paying out 50% of its earnings has far more room to absorb a bad quarter or capital expense without impacting its dividend. The yield alone won’t tell an investor anything about a situation they are actually looking at, which takes us to the second scenario.

The second potential situation is the one where most 6% yields do come from, and it’s the one worth considering the most. If a stock falls drastically, then it is most probably due to the market having started pricing in the troubles behind the scenes, which is what will cause an increase in the yield.

There will no doubt be questions about high yields and any skepticism around these numbers would be fair, but there are some exceptions that should make the doubters feel better. Some sectors, like REITs, for example, carry structurally higher yields, and it has nothing to do with the company being in any kind of trouble. Instead, these companies are required, by law, to distribute roughly 90% of their taxable income. In other words, not only is an elevated yield normal, it’s just how it works.

The same goes for Business Development Companies, which operate under the same kind of rules of needing to distribute taxable income. For their part, MLPs in energy infrastructure also have historically supported higher payouts through long-term contracted cash flow and not earnings that can swing in either direction based on the market.

It always needs to be said that strong businesses that operate in stable industries can also support higher yields. Take a utility company that has regulated revenue and decades of consistent cash generation, which might have a similar 6% yield number as an REIT or BDC, but everything underneath is different.

What does need to hold up across the 6% number is free cash flow coverage, as there has to be enough cash left after capital expenditures are paid out to cover any size dividend. If the payout is being funded by debt, asset sales, or earnings that never actually materialize, this is a warning sign that a dividend cut is on its way.

While yield might get you in the door with a stock, what’s behind the number is going to be the determining factor in whether or not you keep holding it. Ask yourself, has the dividend grown, held flat, or been cut over the last five years? The trajectory of the dividend is arguably more important than the number itself. Then ask yourself what the payout ratio looks like against both earnings and free cash flow. Earnings can be shaped in a way free cash flow cannot, which is why the latter is more critical to understand than the former.

Now ask how much debt is on a company’s balance sheet. What happens to its debt when rates climb? A heavily leveraged company that is paying out a 6% dividend while refinancing debt at higher rates is solving a math problem, and part of the solution to that problem is likely a cut to dividends.

chineseTitle: 6%的股息率真的能持续吗？历史是这样说的
chineseSummary: 6% 的股息收益率听起来像是收入投资者的梦想，但让股票看起来有吸引力的同样数字可能预示着表面之下更令人不安的事情。在购买之前了解其中的差异可以使您的投资组合免遭痛苦的削减。

一旦有人听到“6% 的收益率”这个词，它就会引起很多关注，而且理由是正确的。对于大多数希望从投资组合中获得实际收入和增长的投资者来说，这是一个丰厚的回报。当你看看目前标准普尔 500 指数的平均收益率（约为 1.05%）时，这个数字变得更具吸引力，因此产生比标准普尔指数高四倍的机会无疑很有吸引力。

听到这个收益率数字的挑战在于，您确实需要确保您了解您所获得的收益率。投资者应该注意一些危险信号，了解它们不仅仅是需要考虑的事情，而且在您开始投资之前它们可能是重要的信息。

为什么高收益首先出现

在大多数情况下，计算股息收益率非常容易，因为您只需将年度股息除以股价即可。计算起来非常简单，但现实是公司可以提高股息支付，这是每个投资者都喜欢看到的。然而，如果股价下跌，它会自动推高收益率，而公司无需采取任何行动。

还有另一种情况，通常是6%股息的来源，你必须仔细检查一下。如果一只股票下跌，尤其是下跌得很快，那是因为市场已经开始消化表面之下的错误。收益率上升可能更多的是问题的症状，并不一定是购买股票的理由。

一旦您开始深入研究股息可持续性，您很有可能每次都会得出相同的结论。当收益率接近“正常”水平时，高于大盘的收益率往往会以更高的速度下调。公平地说，这并不是一个硬性规则，但它确实给了我们一些值得考虑的地方，因为那些支付 6% 或更多股价的公司往往是在其现金流水平实际支持的边缘这样做的。

真正能说明问题的是派息率，而将 90% 的收益作为股息派发的公司通常是没有太多缓冲的公司。只需要一个糟糕的季度，一次利率变动，或者一次意外的资本支出，股息就会被削减，投资者就会愤怒不已。一家只支付 50% 收益的公司有更大的空间来吸收糟糕的季度或资本支出，而不影响其股息。仅凭收益率并不能告诉投资者有关他们实际正在关注的情况的任何信息，这将我们带到了第二种情况。

第二种潜在情况是大多数 6% 收益率确实来自的情况，也是最值得考虑的情况。如果一只股票大幅下跌，那么很可能是因为市场已经开始消化幕后的麻烦，这将导致收益率上升。

毫无疑问，人们会对高收益产生疑问，对这些数字的任何怀疑都是公平的，但也有一些例外，应该会让怀疑者感觉好一些。例如，房地产投资信托基金等一些行业的收益率在结构上较高，这与公司陷入任何困境无关。相反，法律要求这些公司分配大约 90% 的应税收入。换句话说，产量增加不仅是正常的，而且也是它的运作方式。

业务发展公司也是如此，它们按照同样需要分配应税收入的规则运营。就能源基础设施领域的 MLP 而言，历史上也通过长期合同现金流支持更高的支出，而不是根据市场向任一方向波动的收益。

需要强调的是，在稳定行业中运营的强大企业也可以支持更高的收益率。以一家公用事业公司为例，该公司的收入受到监管，并且数十年来始终如一地产生现金，其收益率可能与 REIT 或 BDC 类似，均为 6%，但其背后的一切都是不同的。

维持 6% 的数字需要的是自由现金流覆盖率，因为在支付资本支出后必须有足够的现金来支付任何规模的股息。如果支付的资金来自债务、资产出售或从未实际实现的收益，那么这是一个警告信号，表明股息削减即将到来。

虽然收益率可能会让你进入股票大门，但数字背后的内容将成为你是否继续持有股票的决定性因素。问问自己，过去五年股息是增长、持平还是削减？股息的轨迹可以说比数字本身更重要。然后问问自己相对于收益和自由现金流的支付率是多少。收益的形成方式是自由现金流所不能的，这就是为什么后者比前者更重要。

现在询问公司资产负债表上有多少债务。当利率攀升时，其债务会怎样？一家杠杆率很高的公司支付 6% 的股息，同时以更高的利率为债务再融资，这正在解决一个数学问题，而解决该问题的部分方法可能是削减股息。

在数学方面，行业背景也很重要
